articles.title: Quantity and counting
body: Distinct objects can be grouped and counted. Two groups have the same cardinality when every member of one can be paired with exactly one member of the other. Numbers express this abstract relationship independently of the objects counted.
articles.limitations: The written numerals and reading direction are human conventions.

articles.title: Arithmetic and relationships
body: Addition describes combining disjoint finite collections; multiplication describes repeated equal groupings. Equality states that two expressions describe the same value. Subtraction and division reverse these operations when defined.
articles.limitations: Notation does not establish meaning without examples.

articles.title: Geometry and measurement
body: Geometry describes relationships among positions, shapes, distances and angles. A length ratio compares two distances without needing a particular unit. Coordinate systems assign numerical descriptions to positions relative to chosen references.
articles.limitations: Ideal Euclidean geometry is a mathematical model, not a guarantee about physical spacetime.

articles.title: Binary and information
body: A binary alphabet has two distinguishable symbols. In positional base-two notation successive places have weights that are powers of two. A sequence of symbols can encode other structures only when a mapping and boundaries are defined.
articles.limitations: Two physical states do not intrinsically specify orientation, ordering or meaning.

articles.title: Matter and atoms
body: Ordinary matter contains atoms, with nuclei and electrons. The number of protons in a nucleus identifies a chemical element. Isotopes of an element differ in neutron number.
articles.limitations: Atomic images are instrument measurements, not ordinary visible-light photographs.

articles.title: Energy and physical interactions
body: Energy is a measurable quantity that can be transferred and transformed. Interactions govern how matter and radiation change. In suitable isolated systems total energy is conserved.
articles.limitations: A complete physical description requires units, models and domain-specific assumptions.

body: Atoms can form bound structures through electromagnetic interactions. Molecular composition and arrangement influence chemical properties. Water molecules contain two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

articles.title: Stars, galaxies and the Solar System
body: Stars are luminous astronomical bodies powered for much of their lives by nuclear fusion. Galaxies contain stars, gas, dust and other matter. Earth orbits the Sun, one star in the Milky Way galaxy.
articles.limitations: Astronomical images may combine wavelengths or represent different scales.

articles.title: Formation of the Solar System
body: The Sun and its planetary system developed from material in a cloud of gas and dust. Gravity drew material together. A rotating disk surrounded the growing star. In the disk, small solid particles grew into larger bodies through accumulation and some collisions.

Meteorites preserve material from the early Solar System. Observations of disks around young stars provide another way to investigate how planetary systems form. Planet formation concerns the assembly of a planetary body. The emergence of living systems is a separate question.
articles.limitations: This is a simplified formation model; the detailed history of individual bodies remains under investigation.

articles.title: Electromagnetic radiation
body: Electromagnetic radiation can carry energy through empty space. A wave description uses wavelength, the distance between equivalent points such as adjacent crests, and frequency, the number of cycles per unit time. In a vacuum, wavelength multiplied by frequency gives the speed of light. Radio waves have longer wavelengths than the radiation human eyes normally detect.

An instrument can measure intensity in a range of wavelengths and assign colors to display those measurements. The result can show structures invisible to unaided eyes. The display colors then belong to the visualization convention and need the instrument's legend to interpret.
articles.limitations: A wave description is sufficient for these examples. Some measurements require describing transfers of energy in discrete quanta.

articles.title: How stars change
body: Stars form when gravity gathers gas within clouds. If the center becomes sufficiently hot and dense, nuclei can fuse there. For much of the Sun's lifetime, fusion converts hydrogen to helium in the core. Energy transported to the surface escapes as radiation.

Mass influences how a star develops. A star like the Sun can expand into a red giant and eventually leave a compact white dwarf. Some much more massive stars undergo core collapse. Some such collapses produce a supernova, and a neutron star or black hole can remain.
articles.limitations: These are illustrative paths for single stars. Rotation, chemical composition and interactions with companion stars can change events and outcomes.

articles.title: Heat, temperature and matter
body: When two objects at different temperatures make thermal contact, energy tends to move from the warmer object to the cooler one. This transfer due to a temperature difference is called heat. A temperature describes the thermal condition of a system. A large and a small volume of the same liquid can share a temperature while containing different amounts of internal energy.

A phase is a form of matter with uniform physical properties. Ice and liquid water are different phases that can coexist during melting. Whether a substance is solid, liquid or gas can depend on both temperature and pressure. Boiling begins when the vapor pressure of the liquid reaches the surrounding pressure.
articles.limitations: These examples describe familiar materials close to thermal equilibrium. Temperature alone cannot determine the phase without additional conditions.

articles.title: Earth as a planet
body: Earth is a rocky planet with surface oceans and an atmosphere. Below the crust and mostly solid mantle lie a liquid outer core and a solid inner core.

As Earth rotates, most locations periodically move through light and shadow. Earth's rotational axis is tilted relative to the perpendicular to its orbital plane. As the planet travels around the Sun, each hemisphere receives different amounts of sunlight at different times of year.
articles.limitations: Geographic coordinates are conventions; the planet itself provides physical reference features.

articles.title: Water and the water cycle
body: Water circulates through oceans, land, organisms and the atmosphere. Evaporation, condensation, precipitation, runoff and freezing transfer water between reservoirs. These processes depend on energy and environmental conditions.

At a pressure of approximately 101,325 pascals, pure water freezes near 273.15 kelvin and boils near 373.15 kelvin. Pressure and dissolved substances affect these transitions. Water dissolves many substances and participates in the chemistry of known terrestrial life; this does not establish that all possible life requires water.
articles.limitations: Clouds and fog consist of droplets or ice; water vapor is invisible.
articles.status: AI-drafted — source check pending
articles.credit: Centauri Archive editorial draft

articles.title: Atmosphere, climate and geology
body: Earth's atmosphere exchanges energy with the surface and space. Climate describes statistical patterns of weather over time. Geological processes reshape the solid surface, while water and organisms also alter it.
articles.limitations: A single photograph cannot establish a long-term climate trend.
articles.status: AI-drafted — source check pending

articles.title: Water reservoirs and transport
body: Water is distributed across Earth's ocean, inland water bodies, ice, atmosphere, soil and underground spaces. A reservoir can retain water for very different durations depending on its location and the mechanisms moving water into and out of it.

Water can enter the atmosphere from surfaces or plants, return as precipitation, infiltrate the ground, or flow through rivers toward other reservoirs. Solar heating and gravity help drive these transfers. A diagram of the cycle describes recurring processes rather than a single path that every molecule follows.
articles.limitations: A global conceptual diagram cannot describe local water availability, contamination or changes through time.

articles.title: Plate tectonics
body: Earth's rigid outer layer, the lithosphere, includes the crust and uppermost mantle. It is broken into plates that move relative to one another. Where plates separate at ocean ridges, hot material can rise and form new crust. At some convergent boundaries one plate descends into the mantle beneath another. At transform boundaries plates move past one another.

Patterns of earthquakes, volcanic activity and magnetic stripes on the ocean floor support this model. Instruments can also measure the motion of locations on Earth's surface over time. Satellites can observe surface forms such as the East African Rift, where parts of the lithosphere are being pulled apart.
articles.limitations: Surface shape alone does not establish the motion or whether a nearby earthquake is imminent. Plate boundaries can be wide or complex.

articles.title: Cells and metabolism
body: Cells are the basic units of cellular organisms. A cell membrane helps regulate exchanges between the cell and its surroundings. The cell uses ribosomes to assemble proteins, and its internal structures let different processes take place in the same small space.

Bacteria and archaea lack a membrane-bound nucleus. In most eukaryotic cells a nucleus encloses much of the genetic material. Some specialized cells, including mature human red blood cells, lose their nucleus. Mitochondria in eukaryotes and chloroplasts in plants and many algae descend from bacteria that became incorporated into ancestral cells.
Metabolism is the set of chemical reactions in which a cell transforms matter and uses or stores energy. Multicellular organisms distribute some of this work among specialized cells and tissues.
articles.limitations: The cell diagram depicts one general form of animal cell. Membranes, surface structures, organelles and dimensions vary widely.

articles.title: DNA and inheritance
body: In cellular life, deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) carries inherited information. Its strands consist of linked units with four common kinds of bases. The bases occur in sequences, and complementary bases can pair so that each strand can guide the copying of the other.

Changes in base sequence are called mutations. Recombination can rearrange existing variation. Inheritance passes some of this information to new cells and to descendants, while genes and environments both influence how organisms develop.
articles.limitations: Genes operate within cells and environments; they do not determine every trait independently.
articles.status: Source-checked draft — independent human review pending
articles.credit: Centauri Archive editorial draft, written with AI assistance

articles.title: Evolution and biodiversity
body: The frequency of inherited variants can change across generations. One mechanism is natural selection. In a particular environment, individuals with different inherited traits can differ in how many descendants they leave. A variant contributing to greater reproductive success can become more frequent.

Frequency can also change by chance, especially in small populations. That process is genetic drift. Mutation creates new variants, and gene flow moves variants between populations. Shared features and genetic comparisons provide evidence for common ancestry.
articles.limitations: An advantageous trait in one environment can be costly in another. Evolution has no fixed destination. Several mechanisms can operate on the same population at once.

articles.title: Ecosystems and food webs
body: An ecosystem includes organisms and the parts of their surroundings with which they interact. In a food web, a link can trace matter and energy transferred when one organism consumes another. Producers use light or chemical reactions to make organic material. Consumers obtain material and energy by feeding on other organisms or their remains.

Energy enters and leaves local ecosystems. Elements such as carbon and nitrogen can be recycled between living bodies, air, water and sediment. Earth's biosphere comprises the regions where life occurs and includes many connected ecosystems.
articles.limitations: Food webs are variable and interdependent, not simple linear chains.

articles.title: Genes, chromosomes and genomes
body: A genome is the full set of an organism's genetic information. A chromosome is an organized DNA molecule with associated material. A gene is a region of DNA whose information contributes to making a functional RNA or protein.

During protein synthesis, a ribosome reads the sequence in messenger RNA in groups of three bases. These groups specify amino acids or signals, such as when to stop. Other portions of a genome may influence when genes are used or have functions unrelated to making a protein.
Inherited variation can influence how traits develop. The influence can depend on other inherited variants and on conditions during life.
articles.limitations: The organization and interpretation of genomes vary among organisms; the genetic code has some exceptions.

articles.title: Characteristics and origins of known life
body: Earth's cellular organisms maintain boundaries, exchange matter and energy with their surroundings, and carry information that can be inherited. Across generations, populations can evolve. A characteristic shared by living populations need not be expressed by every individual. For example, individual animals that cannot reproduce remain living organisms.

Evidence from ancient rocks and from comparisons among living organisms helps researchers reconstruct some of life's history. How early chemical systems began to maintain themselves, reproduce with variation and evolve remains unsettled. Scientists study several possible pathways; a demonstration that one step can happen leaves the whole historical sequence open.
articles.limitations: The archive describes observed properties of terrestrial life. An agreed universal definition and an independent extraterrestrial example are still missing.
articles.rights: Original project text; publication license pending

articles.title: RNA and proteins
body: Ribonucleic acid, or RNA, is a family of molecules built from linked units. Messenger RNA can carry a copy of information from DNA to a ribosome. Other RNAs help the ribosome read the message and assemble amino acids in sequence. Some RNAs take part in regulation or catalyze chemical reactions.

An amino acid chain can fold into a shape that enables a protein's function. Proteins can provide mechanical structure, carry molecules or accelerate reactions. Changes in a chain or in its surroundings can change how it folds or functions.
articles.limitations: Gene expression and protein assembly vary across organisms and cellular circumstances. This account introduces shared roles at the level needed to read later biology articles.

articles.title: Photosynthesis and cellular respiration
body: In oxygen-producing photosynthesis, cells use light energy to build organic molecules from carbon dioxide. Water supplies electrons and oxygen is released. Plants, algae and cyanobacteria carry out this process. The chloroplasts visible in the leaf micrograph are sites of photosynthesis in plant cells.

During aerobic cellular respiration, cells transfer energy from organic compounds into forms that can support their work. Oxygen accepts electrons at the end of a series of transfers. Cells of photosynthetic plants also respire. Other metabolic pathways enable living cells to obtain energy when oxygen is unavailable.
articles.limitations: This overview describes familiar pathways. Some forms of photosynthesis do not release oxygen, and the availability and use of light and oxygen vary among environments.
articles.rights: Original project text; publication license pending

articles.title: Microorganisms, plants, fungi and animals
body: Microorganisms are organisms studied at scales that often require a microscope. They occur in multiple branches of life. Bacteria and archaea each form major groups, while many other microscopic organisms are eukaryotes, with a different internal cell organization.

Among eukaryotes, many plants use light energy to make organic material. Fungi obtain nutrients from material around them, and many decompose remains or associate with other organisms. Animals are multicellular and acquire organic nutrients from other organisms or their products. Ferns, mushrooms and fish illustrate some of these groups.
articles.limitations: Microorganism describes scale and mode of observation. It is a different kind of category from a lineage. The portraits show examples from many distinct branches, and no one photograph defines a group.
articles.rights: Original project text; publication license pending

articles.title: Biodiversity and extinction
body: Biodiversity includes variation among individuals, among species and among ecosystems. Different species rely on different features of their surroundings. A forest and a coral reef differ in habitat, structure and exchanges of matter and energy, even without counting individual organisms.

A species becomes extinct if its last living members die. A species can also disappear from part of its former range while surviving elsewhere. Human changes to land and oceans, direct exploitation, climate change, pollution and introduced organisms can reduce local or global biodiversity.
articles.limitations: Many species are poorly observed. Estimates of threatened species and of losses depend on observation, definitions, date and the scope of the assessment.
articles.rights: Original project text; publication license pending

articles.title: Human anatomy and physiology
body: Humans are multicellular mammals whose bodies contain specialized tissues and organ systems. Circulation transports materials, respiration exchanges gases, digestion supplies nutrients, and nervous and endocrine systems coordinate functions.
articles.limitations: Teaching models show selected anatomy and do not represent all individual variation.

articles.title: Human development and inheritance
body: Human development includes prenatal growth, infancy, childhood, adolescence and adulthood. Cells divide and differentiate as tissues form and mature. Aging is a variable biological process affected by inherited and environmental factors.
articles.limitations: This summary is biological, not a complete account of individual experience or health.
articles.status: AI-drafted — source check pending

articles.title: Cognition and language
body: Human nervous systems process sensory information and support memory, learning and action. Languages use shared symbolic systems to communicate meaning; spoken, signed and written forms differ in their physical signals.
articles.limitations: Language does not map one-to-one onto universal concepts; cognition is still an active field of research.

articles.title: Organization of the human body
body: The human body can be described at several scales. Molecules form cellular structures; cells cooperate within tissues; tissues form organs; and organs work together in systems. These levels describe relationships within a single living organism.

The heart, blood and blood vessels form a transport system. The respiratory system exchanges gases with the surroundings, while muscles and skeletal structures enable movement. Other systems coordinate responses, process nutrients and maintain internal conditions. Their functions overlap: no organ system is completely independent of the rest of the body.
articles.limitations: The model describes general human biology; individuals differ in anatomy, development and function.

articles.title: Skeleton, joints and muscles
body: Bones support the body, protect some organs and provide surfaces on which muscles can act. A joint is where bones meet. Some joints allow a large range of motion, while others allow very little. Tendons transmit force from muscles to bones. At the elbow, muscle force can bend or straighten the arm.

Skeletal muscle can shorten as its fibers generate tension. Motion usually involves several muscles and coordinated signals from the nervous system. The pottery photograph shows one activity in which the hand's joints, muscles and sense of touch work together.
articles.limitations: An articulated museum skeleton shows the arrangement of bones. It omits living tissue and some features that vary with age, development, disability and individual anatomy.
articles.rights: Original project text; publication license pending

articles.title: Circulation and breathing
body: The heart pumps blood through two connected circuits. The right side sends blood to the lungs. Blood returning from the lungs enters the left side, which pumps it through vessels to the rest of the body. Small vessels called capillaries exchange materials with surrounding tissues.

Air enters the lungs during inhalation. At small air sacs called alveoli, oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide moves from the blood into air that can be exhaled. The blood transports oxygen to tissues and carries carbon dioxide away. Breathing and cellular respiration describe different processes.
articles.limitations: The diagram shows the flow of blood after birth at a simplified scale. The fetal circulation uses different pathways, and real blood vessels form branching networks.
articles.rights: Original project text; publication license pending

articles.title: Digestion and nutrient absorption
body: Digestion changes food into forms the body can use. Teeth break food into smaller pieces. In the stomach and intestines, movement mixes the contents with fluids, and enzymes split many large molecules. The liver makes bile, which helps process fats, and the pancreas supplies several digestive enzymes.

Much of the absorption of nutrients takes place across the wall of the small intestine. The large intestine absorbs water, and its microorganisms transform some compounds that reach it. Circulation distributes absorbed materials to tissues.
articles.limitations: Food and meals vary across communities and individuals. These descriptions explain physiology without specifying a diet or treating one daily practice as universal.
articles.rights: Original project text; publication license pending

Transfer of materials across an interface such as the intestinal lining.

articles.title: Nervous system and senses
body: The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system. Nerves connect it to much of the body. Neurons convey signals through changes in electrical activity and often communicate with other cells using chemical signals. These networks support movement, coordination and the processing of information.

Receptor cells respond to particular kinds of input. Cells in the retina respond to light. Vibrations transmitted through the ear can move sensory cells in the inner ear and produce signals. Other receptors respond to mechanical force, chemicals or temperature. Signals from many receptors are combined during perception.
articles.limitations: The eye photograph shows an external part of the eye. The ear record depicts a model and the microscopy record shows rat neurons. Human sensory experience and abilities vary.
articles.rights: Original project text; publication license pending

articles.title: Immune function and homeostasis
body: Homeostasis describes regulated conditions in the body, such as temperature, staying within ranges compatible with function. When body temperature rises, evaporation of sweat can remove heat. This is a feedback process because the response changes the condition that helped trigger it.

Several systems help protect tissue from damage and infection. Skin and other barriers restrict entry. Immune cells can respond to signs of damage or foreign material; some mount more targeted responses. Antibodies can bind specific targets, and some immune cells persist after a response, supporting a faster response on later encounters.
articles.limitations: Normal ranges and responses vary across people and circumstances. These examples describe basic physiology, and immune activity can also damage healthy tissue.

articles.title: Reproduction, development and variation
body: In sexual reproduction, fertilization joins an egg and sperm, forming a cell called a zygote. As cells divide, groups specialize into tissues. During development in the uterus, the placenta supports exchanges of materials between the pregnant individual and the developing organism. Ultrasound imaging uses echoes to show some structures before birth.

Human bodies continue to change after birth. Genes, environments and lived conditions influence development and aging. Individual variation includes differences in body proportions, sensory abilities and rates of change. Images of people at different life stages can show examples of variation.
articles.limitations: Life stages are descriptive and can be defined differently by culture and purpose. A single ultrasound and a single group portrait show individuals at particular times.
articles.rights: Original project text; publication license pending

articles.title: Human history and communities
body: Human communities have changed over long periods through migration, cooperation, conflict, environmental changes and invention. Archaeology, historical records and oral traditions provide different evidence about the past.

The existing archive chronology traces the emergence of Homo sapiens in Africa hundreds of thousands of years ago, independent agricultural traditions beginning roughly twelve thousand years ago, early writing systems in several societies more than five thousand years ago, and industrialization in parts of the world beginning in the eighteenth century. These are approximate milestones, not a universal timeline. Sputnik 1 orbited Earth in 1957; humans first landed on the Moon in 1969.
articles.limitations: No single region or linear timeline adequately represents human history.
articles.status: AI-drafted — source check pending
articles.credit: Centauri Archive editorial draft
articles.rights: Original project text; publication license pending

articles.title: Institutions, exchange and ideas
body: Humans form institutions to coordinate activity, transmit knowledge, allocate resources and resolve disputes. Communities use diverse political, economic, ethical and philosophical systems. These systems change over time.
articles.limitations: Descriptions of institutions must distinguish documented practice from ideals and contested judgments.
articles.status: AI-drafted — source check pending

articles.title: Agriculture and engineering
body: Agriculture involves managing organisms and environments to produce food and other resources. Engineering applies knowledge and design to create systems that serve specified purposes under constraints.
articles.limitations: Technological development brings benefits, costs and unequal impacts.
articles.status: AI-drafted — source check pending

articles.title: Computing and artificial intelligence
body: Computers transform encoded information according to specified operations. Artificial intelligence includes computational methods for tasks such as pattern recognition, prediction and planning. Some systems learn statistical relationships from data.
articles.limitations: Capabilities and limitations vary by system; machine output is not automatically correct or conscious.

articles.title: Flight and space exploration
body: Aircraft use aerodynamic forces to travel through an atmosphere. Spacecraft operate beyond much of Earth's atmosphere and can use propulsion to change their motion. Human missions and robotic instruments have extended observation beyond Earth.
articles.limitations: Historical mission photographs document particular achievements, not a general measure of technological capability.

articles.title: Art, music and daily experience
body: Humans express experience through visual forms, sound, movement, stories, craft and play. Everyday practices communicate cultural knowledge as well as serving practical needs.

People live in cities, towns, villages, farms and mobile settlements. Homes, meals, clothing and relationships differ with environment, resources and social practices. Knowledge is transmitted by speech, signing, writing, teaching, observation and performance. Cultures continue to change; no country's customs represent humanity as a whole. Cooperation coexists with inequality and conflict. Communities should be able to describe their own practices, and restrictions on sensitive cultural materials deserve respect.
articles.limitations: Meaning and aesthetic experience vary across people and cultures; an image or sound is only a partial record.

articles.title: Centauri Archive and interstellar messages
body: Centauri Archive is an independent research project developing a durable, intelligible record of Earth. Its development package and photographic collection are not a flight-qualified artifact. Voyager's Golden Record provides a historical precedent for interstellar messages.
articles.limitations: Fermi Explorer integration is proposed, not approved. Physical survival and interpretation by unknown readers remain open engineering and research questions.
